nodes.label: Nancy Christie
nodes.date_label: A Full-Orbed Christianity, with Michael Gauvreau (1996) · Engendering the State (2000) · Christian Churches and Their Peoples, with Michael Gauvreau (2010)
nodes.description: A Canadian historian of family, welfare and religion. Engendering the State investigates changes in the gendered foundations of social provision. Her work with Michael Gauvreau places churches within the making of modern social policy. In her 2009 intervention on the liberal order framework, she accepts its capacity to connect historical studies but challenges its periodization and emphasis on the state. She argues that a property-based account of individualism obscures women’s participation through households, churches and voluntary associations. This is a proposed revision of the framework, rather than a rejection of all its questions.

nodes.label: J. R. Miller
nodes.date_label: Skyscrapers Hide the Heavens (1989) · Shingwauk’s Vision (1996) · Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009)
nodes.description: A settler historian of Indigenous–newcomer relations, residential schools and treaty-making in Canada. His national syntheses brought government and church records together with published scholarship and interview evidence. Celia Haig-Brown’s 1997 review of Shingwauk’s Vision credits its breadth and research while questioning how examples drawn across places and decades can flatten differences among nations and schools. She also challenges its claims to balance and its treatment of resistance. This entry retains that criticism alongside the synthesis. It describes scholarly method and responsibility without reproducing testimony or community knowledge.

nodes.label: Bruce G. Trigger
nodes.date_label: The Children of Aataentsic (1976) · Natives and Newcomers (1985) · A History of Archaeological Thought (1989)
nodes.description: A Canadian archaeologist and ethnohistorian whose work connects material evidence with documentary history. The Children of Aataentsic and Natives and Newcomers reconsider earlier accounts of Wendat/Huron history and colonial encounters. His 1986 historiographical essay discusses bringing interdisciplinary ethnohistory into national history. That project does not escape Indigenous criticism. In her 1999 dissertation, Emma LaRocque criticizes his foreword to Georges Sioui’s Autohistory as limiting Indigenous historical authority, and includes Trigger in a cross-cultural approach that she sees as improved on earlier racism yet still capable of distancing and Othering its subjects.

nodes.label: Caroline Walker Bynum
nodes.date_label: Jesus as Mother: essay collection (1982) · Holy Feast and Holy Fast (1987) · Fragmentation and Redemption (1991)
nodes.description: A historian of medieval European religion whose studies make gender, embodiment and material practices questions of historical interpretation. In her 2012 scholarly autobiography, she explains the movement from studying maternal imagery used by male religious authorities to comparing writings by and about religious women. She resists both a simple scale of women’s status and explanations that make religious practice merely pathological or compensatory. Her method seeks cultural assumptions while preserving incompatible voices and the strangeness of the past. Those retrospective arguments support this entry; the selected monographs are not presented as fully read.

nodes.label: Barbara H. Rosenwein
nodes.date_label: Negotiating Space (1999) · “Worrying about Emotions in History” (2002) · Emotional Communities in the Early Middle Ages (2006)
nodes.description: A medieval historian whose studies of property and immunity developed into an inquiry into the history of emotions. Her 2002 article proposes overlapping emotional communities in place of a single story of movement from uncontrolled medieval feeling to modern restraint. Her 2010 interview also questions a regime/refuge model that too sharply separates power from emotional alternatives. Reddy’s answer allowing plural regimes remains a distinct qualification, rather than being erased by that objection. This entry uses the atlas’s earlier bounded readings of the article and interview; the medieval monographs supply separate bibliographic milestones.

nodes.label: Joanna Bourke
nodes.date_label: Dismembering the Male (1996) · An Intimate History of Killing (1999) · Fear: A Cultural History (2005)
nodes.description: A historian of modern Britain and of bodily experience, violence and emotion. Dismembering the Male studies men’s bodies and masculinity during and after the Great War; An Intimate History of Killing asks how combatants experienced the act of killing. Her later cultural histories investigate how pain and fear acquire meanings in changing social settings. In her 2023 lecture on dementia, she asks how historical narratives shape personhood and warns that making vulnerable people visible can also compromise their dignity. The lecture supplies a bounded methodological example, rather than a reading of all her books.

nodes.label: Keith Thomas
nodes.date_label: “History and Anthropology” (1963) · Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971) · Man and the Natural World (1983)
nodes.description: A social and cultural historian of early modern England. Religion and the Decline of Magic investigates beliefs that modern readers may dismiss while asking why they made sense within past social worlds. Jan Machielsen and Michelle Pfeffer’s 2023 reassessment reads the book as both an engagement with anthropology and an accumulation of historically particular voices. They also show why its categories and account of decline remain contested, including Hildred Geertz’s criticism of its assumptions about magic. This named reading keeps its achievement and its limits together; the selected books are not claimed read in full.
nodes.representative_figures_and_works: “History and Anthropology” (1963); Religion and the Decline of Magic (1971); Man and the Natural World (1983); The Ends of Life (2009).
nodes.scope_note: Interpretation uses Machielsen and Pfeffer’s opening and selected sections II–III, plus the existing limited Stone reading. Thomas’s 1963 article is metadata-only and all selected books are unread in full. Geertz’s original criticism and Thomas’s original reply are not newly read. The account does not reduce Thomas’s work to one anthropological theory.

nodes.label: J. H. Elliott
nodes.date_label: Imperial Spain, 1469–1716 (1963) · “A Europe of Composite Monarchies” (1992) · Empires of the Atlantic World (2006)
nodes.description: A historian of early modern Spain, Europe and the Americas. His work moves between political choices within composite monarchies and comparisons across imperial settings. In his Making History interview, he explains comparison as a way to challenge national exceptionalisms and discusses the autonomy possible within composite polities. Empires of the Atlantic World places British and Spanish America within a comparative inquiry. This entry uses bounded interview extracts and institutional bibliographies; it does not infer a global framework from the mere presence of two empires or present the selected books as fully read.

nodes.label: John M. MacKenzie
nodes.date_label: Propaganda and Empire (1984) · Imperialism and Popular Culture: edited collection (1986) · The Empire of Nature (1988)
nodes.description: A historian of empire whose cultural and environmental studies connect imperial power with life in Britain and overseas. As founding editor of Studies in Imperialism, he helped make metropolitan culture a central problem of imperial history. Alison Frank Johnson reads The Empire of Nature as connecting hunting and conservation to British rule in Africa and India. His work is also contested: Edward Said’s review of Catherine Hall criticizes an approach associated with MacKenzie that treats culture as propaganda. That specific criticism is retained without making MacKenzie’s method identical to Hall’s or treating cultural imperial history as membership in British cultural studies.

nodes.label: Callum G. Brown
nodes.date_label: Religion and Society in Scotland since 1707: listed edition 2 (1997) · The Death of Christian Britain: first edition (2001) · Postmodernism for Historians (2005) · Religion and Society in Twentieth-Century Britain (2006)
nodes.description: A social and cultural historian of religion and nonreligion in Scotland, Britain and other western societies. The Death of Christian Britain challenges a long, gradual account of secularization by emphasizing a rupture in the 1960s. In his Glasgow research statement, Brown describes the gendered and discursive character of religious identity and advocates combining documentary research, oral history, quantitative methods and discourse analysis. These are his stated methods and interpretations, not a consensus account of secularization. His Canadian roster context remains a comparison with Canadian scholarship rather than a claim that the British book is a Canadian national history.

Glasgow’s narrative says 2000 for Death, while its 2001/2009 bibliography and first-edition publisher listing support 2001; the discrepancy is recorded. The garbled citation key is retained only in the research bridge and does not change the historian’s identity.

edges.relationship: Challenges the framework’s timing, statism and property-based account of individualism.
edges.evidence_note: Complete institutional essay re-read, especially paragraphs beginning The first issue, Since liberalism, and I think that a renewed emphasis. Supports a qualified critique, not a rejection of the framework’s synthesizing value.

edges.relationship: Makes women’s associational and household activity part of the explanation of liberal rule.
edges.evidence_note: 2009 essay, final three substantive paragraphs; JSTOR displayed introduction opening supplements the welfare research question. No claim that women uniformly benefited from liberalism.

edges.relationship: Treats churches and voluntary associations as sites where liberal values were made and contested.
edges.evidence_note: 2009 essay, paragraph beginning Probably the most important site. Her intervention supplies this claim; the coauthored books are not presented as freshly read.

edges.relationship: Builds national syntheses of relations and residential schooling whose scale also raises questions about local and national difference.
edges.evidence_note: Haig-Brown, printed pp. 100–101: broad archival/interview synthesis and criticism of homogenizing examples. The arrow records a contested contribution, not Indigenous authorship or endorsement by communities.

edges.relationship: Makes church responsibility and its relation to state policy central problems in residential-school history.
edges.evidence_note: Haig-Brown, printed p. 100 on assigning responsibility, p. 101 on balanced accounts. Her objections accompany the contribution; this is an addition to the religion field, not an assertion of agreement with a secularization thesis.

edges.relationship: Argues for interdisciplinary ethnohistory and its integration into national historical writing.
edges.evidence_note: Existing bounded reading of the 1986 essay opening only, as documented in the baseline source note. No fresh full reading or claim that ethnohistory supplies Indigenous authority.

edges.relationship: Brings archaeological and ethnographic work into contact with documentary history.
edges.evidence_note: 1986 essay opening as previously documented: an interdisciplinary research undertaking, not equivalence among disciplines or endorsement of a uniform ethnographic method.

edges.relationship: Criticizes his containment of Sioui’s intervention and the distancing effects of his cross-cultural historiography.
edges.evidence_note: LaRocque’s 1999 dissertation, existing documented reading at PDF pp. 135–136 (foreword) and 249 (cross-cultural approach). edges.relationship: Challenges reduction of medieval women’s religiosity to pathology or a single measure of status.

edges.relationship: Insists that cultural interpretation preserve conflicting voices and the historical foreignness of the past.
